title: Rate limiting
subtitle: A rate limit says no early and cheaply, so one noisy client cannot take your service down for everyone else.

c.v: This story is made up, but it is common. A small company sells a public API for sending text messages. Most customers send a few requests a second.
One Monday, a new customer starts a data import. Their script has a bug: when a request is slow, it
at once, in a loop, with no wait. Soon this one customer sends 3,000 requests a second.
The API servers pass every request to the database. The database slows down, so requests get slower. Slower requests make the script retry even more.
Within ten minutes, every customer sees
. The team blocks the customer by hand, and things recover. Then the next question comes: "Why could one customer do this at all?"
. The service said yes to every request until it could not say anything.

A rate limit is a rule like "each API key may make 100 requests a minute". The service counts requests. When a client goes over the limit, the service rejects the extra requests at once, before doing any real work.
A rate limit protects you in three ways:
One client, a bug or an attack cannot use all your capacity.
You do not pay for work that nobody planned for.
A fast, cheap "no" is better than a slow "yes" that ends in a timeout. Rejecting early keeps the service healthy for everyone else.
Picture a bucket of tokens for each client. Each request takes one token. Tokens drip back in at a fixed rate, up to the size of the bucket. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.

It is cheap and easy to explain to customers.
But the edges are weak. With a limit of 100 a minute, a client can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00. That is 200 requests in two seconds.
stores the time of every request. To decide, it counts the times in the last 60 seconds. It is exact, but it stores one entry per request, which uses a lot of memory for busy clients.
keeps only two counters: this minute and last minute. It guesses the rate by weighting last minute's count by how much of it is still inside the window.
Cloudflare gives an example. The limit is 50 a minute. Last minute had 42 requests, and this minute has 18 so far, 15 seconds in. The estimate is 42 × 0.75 + 18 = 49.5, just under the limit.
It is only an estimate. But on 400 million requests, Cloudflare found just 0.003% were wrongly allowed or wrongly limited.
If each server counts in its own memory, the limit multiplies. With 20 servers and a limit of 100, a user can make up to 2,000 requests.
So most teams keep counters in a shared store like Redis. Be careful with races. If you
a key and set its expiry in a separate step, a crash between them can leave the key with no expiry. Redis suggests

A shared store adds a network call to every request, so it can become a bottleneck. Envoy's answer is a separate rate limit service, plus a local token bucket on each proxy. Its reference service uses Redis. The local limit absorbs large bursts and cuts the load on the shared service.
What if the limiter itself fails, because of a bug or because Redis goes down? Stripe's advice is to

The limiter should never become the outage.

The service knows the user, their plan and how costly each call is. A search can cost much more than a read by ID.
Our advice is to use both: a coarse limit at the gateway and finer limits in the service.
A per-user limit keeps things fair. A global limit protects a shared resource, such as the database, whoever the traffic comes from.
Stripe runs four kinds. A request rate limiter caps each user's requests per second. A concurrent requests limiter caps how many requests can run at once, such as 20. Two
protect the whole system: one keeps capacity for critical requests, and the other sheds traffic when workers are overloaded.

Choose the key with care: API key, user, account or IP address. Many users can share one office IP address.

Put limits in your API docs. Send 429 with

Alert when limits fire a lot. It can mean an attack, a client bug or a limit that is too low.

Treat limiting a customer as a product decision, with an owner and a clear process. In 2023, an unapproved throttle applied by hand made one Cloudflare customer's site unusable. It stayed on for almost 13 hours. Afterwards, Cloudflare said such actions would need several levels of approval.
Check your own clients: they should back off with
"Add a token bucket rate limiter to this API, per API key, stored in Redis. Use a Lua script so the check and the update happen together. Return 429 with Retry-After."
"Write tests for the limiter: a burst up to the bucket size passes, the next request gets 429, and one request passes after one refill interval."
"Make the limiter fail open if Redis is down or slow for more than 20 ms. Log and count every fail-open."

q.v: A token bucket holds 10 tokens and adds 2 tokens a second. The bucket is full. A client sends 15 requests at once. How many go through right away?

why.v: The bucket holds 10 tokens, so 10 requests go through. The other 5 are rejected. New tokens then arrive at 2 a second.

q.v: Your limit is 100 requests per minute with a fixed window. What is the worst case?

options.v: About 200 requests in two seconds, around the edge of two windows.

why.v: A client can send 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next.

q.v: You run 20 servers. Each keeps its own in-memory limit of 100 requests per minute per user. What is the real limit for one user?

why.v: Each server counts alone. A user whose requests spread over all 20 servers can make 20 × 100.

q.v: What should a well-behaved client do when it gets 429 with "Retry-After: 30"?

options.v: Retry at once, in a loop.
Wait at least 30 seconds before it tries again.
Treat it as a bug in the server and give up forever.

why.v: Retry-After tells the client how long to wait. Retrying sooner only adds load.

q.v: Your shared Redis for rate limits goes down. What does Stripe advise?

options.v: Block all requests until Redis is back.
Fail open, so a limiter problem does not break real requests.

why.v: The limiter protects the service. It should not become a new way for the service to fail.
